sections.title: Basic Concept of Prepositions and Conjunctions
sections.content: Prepositions are words that show the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another part of the sentence. Conjunctions are words that connect two words, phrases, or clauses. In competitive examinations, identifying their correct usage is very important.

sections.title: Basic Prepositions of Time and Place
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the sentence is talking about time or place. Step 2: Choose the correct preposition. Step 3: Apply the common rules. For Time: 'at' is used for exact time (at 5 PM), 'on' is used for days or dates (on Monday), and 'in' is used for months, years, or longer periods (in July, in 2025). For Place: 'in' is used for large areas (in India), 'at' is used for specific points (at the station), and 'on' is used for surfaces (on the table).

sections.title: Using Since and For
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the sentence refers to the starting point of time or the duration. Step 2: If it indicates the starting point, use 'since'. Step 3: If it indicates a duration, use 'for'. Example: He has lived here since 2020. He has lived here for five years.

sections.title: Basic Coordinating Conjunctions
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether two similar words or clauses are being connected. Step 2: Choose the correct conjunction. 'And' is used for addition, 'but' is used for contrast, 'or' is used for alternatives, and 'so' is used to show result. Example: She studied hard, so she passed the exam.

sections.title: Basic Subordinating Conjunctions
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the main clause and the dependent clause. Step 2: Choose the conjunction according to the meaning of cause or contrast. 'Because' shows cause, while 'although' shows contrast. Example: Although it was raining, we went outside.

sections.title: Between vs Among
sections.content: Step 1: Check how many people or things are involved in the relationship. Step 2: Use 'between' when there are two. Step 3: Use 'among' when there are more than two. Example: The money was divided between two friends. The sweets were shared among the children.

sections.title: Beside vs Besides
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the meaning is 'next to' or 'in addition to'. Step 2: If the meaning is 'next to' or physically near, use 'beside'. Step 3: If the meaning is 'in addition to', use 'besides'. Example: He sat beside me. Besides English, she knows Hindi.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Using incorrect time prepositions. 2. Confusing 'since' and 'for'. 3. Using 'between' and 'among' incorrectly. 4. Treating 'beside' and 'besides' as the same.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Prepositions describe time, place, or relationships, while conjunctions connect parts of a sentence. By remembering the correct rules and understanding the meaning, their correct usage can be easily identified.

tricks.title: Time Preposition Rule
tricks.explanation: Use 'at' for exact time, 'on' for day or date, and 'in' for month or year.
tricks.example: At 7 AM, On Sunday, In December.

tricks.title: Since vs For Shortcut
tricks.example: She has worked here since 2021. She has worked here for three years.

tricks.title: Surface Rule
tricks.explanation: Use 'on' when something is placed on a surface.
tricks.example: The book is on the table.

tricks.title: Between Rule
tricks.explanation: Use 'between' when referring to two persons or things.
tricks.example: The match was between India and Australia.

tricks.title: Among Rule
tricks.explanation: Use 'among' when referring to more than two persons or things.
tricks.example: The teacher distributed books among the students.

tricks.title: Beside Meaning Trick
tricks.explanation: Beside means 'next to' or physically near.

tricks.title: Cause Conjunction Trick
tricks.explanation: Use 'because' when the sentence shows a reason.
tricks.example: She stayed home because she was sick.

tricks.title: Contrast Conjunction Trick
tricks.example: He tried hard, but he failed.
